H1.text: A bowl of rice, a spoon of ghee, a cup of dal. Three very different foods.

H2.text: Yet your cells can burn all three for energy, in one shared pathway.

H3.text: Diya wondered about this in the kitchen. She asked: how much energy does one sugar molecule really give? And does every food use oxygen the same way?

H4.text: Here is the short answer. One glucose can give thirty-eight ATP. And the gas trade changes with the food.

H5.text: By the end, you will know the respiratory balance sheet, the amphibolic pathway, and the respiratory quotient.

B1.text: First, what is a balance sheet?

B2.text: A balance sheet counts what comes in and what goes out, like a bank statement.

B3.text: For respiration, we count the ATP made from one glucose molecule. ATP is the cell's energy coin. Glucose and oxygen go in. Carbon dioxide, water and ATP come out.

Z1.text: Let's zoom in to where most of this ATP is made.

Z2.text: A plant cell has many mitochondria. Glycolysis happens outside them, in the cytoplasm.

Z3.text: Zoom closer. Inside one mitochondrion, the Krebs cycle runs in the matrix, the jelly in the middle.

Z4.text: Zoom to the inner membrane. Here the electron transport system turns NADH and FADH two into ATP. Each NADH gives three ATP. Each FADH two gives two.

L1.text: But this count works only if four things are true. Let's check them.

L2.text: One. The pathway runs in order: glycolysis, then the Krebs cycle, then the electron transport system.

L3.text: Two. The NADH made in glycolysis enters the mitochondria and makes ATP there.

L4.text: Three. No middle product leaves the pathway to build something else.

L5.text: Four. Only glucose is respired. No other food enters halfway.

L6.text: If all four hold, one glucose gives a net gain of thirty-eight ATP. But in a living cell these rules are not always true. So thirty-eight is a calculated figure.

C1.text: Now compare this with fermentation, which runs without oxygen.

C2.text: Fermentation breaks glucose only partly. Aerobic respiration breaks it completely, to carbon dioxide and water.

C3.text: Fermentation gives a net gain of only two ATP per glucose. Aerobic respiration gives many more.

C4.text: And in fermentation, NADH turns back into NAD plus slowly. In aerobic respiration this happens very fast.

D1.text: Now, rule three said nothing leaves the pathway. In a real cell, things leave all the time.

D2.text: Glucose is the favourite fuel. But fats and proteins can be respired too.

D3.text: Fats first split into glycerol and fatty acids. Fatty acids become acetyl CoA. Glycerol becomes PGAL, a three-carbon sugar of glycolysis.

D4.text: Proteins split into amino acids. Each one enters as pyruvate, as acetyl CoA, or inside the Krebs cycle.

D5.text: Breaking food down is catabolism. Building new molecules is anabolism. When the cell needs fatty acids, it pulls acetyl CoA out of the pathway to build them.

D6.text: So one pathway both breaks down and builds up. That is why it is called an amphibolic pathway, not just a catabolic one.

U1.text: Now, the third idea. Respiration trades oxygen for carbon dioxide.

U2.text: The respiratory quotient, or RQ, is the volume of carbon dioxide given out divided by the volume of oxygen used.

U3.text: For glucose, six carbon dioxide come out for six oxygen taken in. Six divided by six is one.

U4.text: For a fat like tripalmitin, two molecules give out one hundred and two carbon dioxide and use one hundred and forty-five oxygen. The RQ is about zero point seven.

U5.text: For proteins, the RQ is about zero point nine. Real cells usually burn a mix. Pure fats or pure proteins are never the only fuel.

U6.text: Your turn. A seed burns mostly fat. Is its RQ more than one, or less than one? Pause and decide.

U7.text: Less than one! Fats hold little oxygen, so they need more oxygen for each carbon dioxide they release.

T1.text: Remember this. RQ is carbon dioxide out, divided by oxygen in.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Let's count the thirty-eight ATP from one glucose.

W2.text: Glycolysis gives two ATP and two NADH. Two NADH times three is six. Two plus six is eight.

W3.text: The link step, pyruvate to acetyl CoA, gives two NADH. Two times three is six ATP.

W4.text: The Krebs cycle turns twice. Two ATP, six NADH and two FADH two: two plus eighteen plus four is twenty-four. Eight plus six plus twenty-four makes thirty-eight.

X2.text: Many students think every living cell always makes exactly thirty-eight ATP per glucose.

X3.text: But thirty-eight is a theoretical figure. It holds only if the four assumptions are true, and in a real cell they often are not.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As statement and match questions on the ATP count, the amphibolic pathway and RQ values.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Match each substrate with its RQ. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Carbohydrate one, tripalmitin zero point seven, protein zero point nine.

A2.text: Glucose gives six carbon dioxide for six oxygen, so its RQ is exactly one.

A3.text: Tripalmitin gives one hundred and two for one hundred and forty-five, about zero point seven. Proteins are about zero point nine.
